column7: How does TLS 1.3 differ from TLS 1.2 in its handshake process?
column8: TLS 1.3 reduces the handshake from two round-trips to one (1-RTT) by combining the ClientHello and key-share into a single flight. It removes support for static RSA key exchange and legacy cipher suites such as CBC-mode ciphers, retaining only AEAD algorithms like AES-128-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305. The server responds with its key-share, encrypted extensions, and finished message in one flight, allowing application data to flow after just one round-trip. TLS 1.3 also supports 0-RTT resumption, where cached pre-shared keys let clients send early data before the handshake completes, at the cost of reduced replay protection.
column9: TLS 1.3, defined in RFC 8446, redesigns the handshake to complete in a single round-trip (1-RTT) instead of the two round-trips required by TLS 1.2. The client sends a ClientHello message that includes supported cipher suites and one or more key-share entries (typically ECDHE). The server selects a cipher suite, responds with its own key-share, and derives handshake keys immediately. All cipher suites in TLS 1.3 use AEAD constructions; supported algorithms include AES-128-GCM, AES-256-GCM, and ChaCha20-Poly1305. Static RSA and Diffie-Hellman key exchanges, CBC-mode ciphers, and MD5/SHA-1 hash functions are removed. A 0-RTT mode allows session resumption with pre-shared keys (PSK), enabling clients to send early application data in the first flight, though this data is not forward-secret and is susceptible to replay attacks.

column7: Compare the time complexity of quicksort and mergesort, including worst-case scenarios and when each is preferred.
column8: Quicksort has an average-case time complexity of O(n log n) and a worst-case of O(n²), which occurs when the pivot selection is poor (e.g. already sorted input with first-element pivot). Mergesort guarantees O(n log n) in all cases — best, average, and worst — because it always divides the array in half. However, mergesort requires O(n) auxiliary space for the merge step, while quicksort operates in-place with O(log n) stack space on average. Quicksort is generally preferred for in-memory sorting due to better cache locality and lower constant factors, while mergesort is preferred for linked lists (no random access needed) and external sorting (sequential access patterns). In practice, many libraries use hybrid approaches like Timsort (merge + insertion sort) or introsort (quicksort + heapsort fallback).

column7: Explain the CAP theorem in distributed systems, how it applies to databases like MongoDB, Cassandra, and Spanner, and what trade-offs each makes.
column8:
The CAP theorem states that a distributed system can only guarantee two of three properties simultaneously: Consistency (all nodes see the same data at the same time), Availability (every request receives a response), and Partition tolerance (the system continues to operate despite network partitions). Since network partitions are inevitable in distributed systems, the real choice is between consistency and availability during a partition.

MongoDB is a CP system by default: during a network partition, it elects a new primary and rejects writes on the minority side, prioritising consistency over availability. However, with read preferences set to secondary, it can trade consistency for availability on reads.

Cassandra is an AP system: it uses a peer-to-peer architecture with tunable consistency levels. With eventual consistency, it remains available during partitions. Setting consistency level to QUORUM or ALL moves it toward CP at the cost of availability.

Google Spanner aims to provide all three properties in practice through TrueTime (GPS and atomic clock synchronisation), achieving external consistency (linearisability) with high availability. It is technically CP but engineered so that partitions are extremely rare within Google's network, making it effectively CA in practice.

In practice, partition tolerance is mandatory for distributed systems, so the trade-off is between C and A. MongoDB uses a single-primary replica set architecture and is generally classified as CP: if a partition separates the primary from the majority, writes fail on the minority side until a new primary is elected. Cassandra uses a masterless ring architecture and is classified as AP with tunable consistency; at consistency level ONE it favours availability, while at QUORUM it provides stronger consistency guarantees. Google Spanner uses synchronous replication, Paxos consensus, and a GPS/atomic-clock-based timestamp system called TrueTime to provide external consistency (the strongest form of consistency) with high availability, making it effectively CP, though Google's private network infrastructure minimises partition events to near zero.

Explain the CAP theorem in distributed systems, how it applies to databases like MongoDB, Cassandra, and Spanner, and what trade-offs each makes.||The CAP theorem states that a distributed system can only guarantee two of three properties simultaneously: Consistency (all nodes see the same data at the same time), Availability (every request receives a response), and Partition tolerance (the system continues to operate despite network partitions). Since network partitions are inevitable in distributed systems, the real choice is between consistency and availability during a partition.

MongoDB is a CP system by default: during a network partition, it elects a new primary and rejects writes on the minority side, prioritising consistency over availability. However, with read preferences set to secondary, it can trade consistency for availability on reads.

Cassandra is an AP system: it uses a peer-to-peer architecture with tunable consistency levels. With eventual consistency, it remains available during partitions. Setting consistency level to QUORUM or ALL moves it toward CP at the cost of availability.

Google Spanner aims to provide all three properties in practice through TrueTime (GPS and atomic clock synchronisation), achieving external consistency (linearisability) with high availability. It is technically CP but engineered so that partitions are extremely rare within Google's network, making it effectively CA in practice.

column7: Is water wet?
column8: Whether water is wet depends on definition. If wet means having water on a surface, water itself is not wet — it makes other things wet. If wet means being a liquid or being in contact with liquid, then water is wet. There is no single scientifically agreed-upon answer.
column9: Wetness is typically defined as the condition of being covered or saturated with a liquid, most commonly water. In physics and chemistry, wetness relates to the ability of a liquid to maintain contact with a solid surface through adhesion and surface tension. Whether water itself is considered wet is a topic of informal debate with no definitive scientific consensus.

column7: What is a closure in programming?
column8: A closure is a function that captures the lexical scope in which it was defined. This means the function retains access to variables from its enclosing scope even after that scope has finished executing. Closures are not the same as anonymous functions — a named function can also be a closure if it references free variables from an outer scope.
column9: In programming, a closure is a technique for implementing lexically scoped name binding in a language with first-class functions. A closure is a record storing a function together with an environment: a mapping of each free variable of the function with the value or reference to which the name was bound when the closure was created. A closure, unlike a plain function, allows the function to access those captured variables through the closure's copies of their values or references, even when the function is invoked outside their scope.
